newsitem.title: UK: Thousands march on N. Ireland's "Bloody Sunday".
newsitem.headline: Thousands march on N. Ireland's "Bloody Sunday".

text.p: Catholics prepared to march on Sunday to mark the 25th anniversary of the "Bloody Sunday" slaying of demonstrators by British troops that propelled Northern Ireland to unresolved conflict.

The marchers, following the same fateful route from the Catholic bogside area of Londonderry to the city's walls, will lay wreaths and add their voices to calls for a new inquiry into one of the darkest days of Northern Ireland history.

Gerry Adams, head of the IRA guerrillas' political wing, Sinn Fein, told Sky Television that "Bloody Sunday is an open wound, a Sunday which never ended" and urged a reluctant British government to examine new theories about the killings.

An official 1972 investigation exonerated British paratroopers who believed that they were under fire from Irish Republican Army guerrillas attached to an 80,000-strong Catholic civil rights demonstration.

British Prime Minister John Major last week called Bloody Sunday a terrible tragedy but stopped far short of ordering a new investigation into the killings - a 14th man died of his wounds after the shooting.

The killings stunned the largely pro-Irish 40 percent Catholic minority and sent outraged youths hurrying to join the IRA's continuing guerrilla campaign to end British rule and join Northern Ireland with the Irish republic.

The 25th anniversary is being marked against a background of a new IRA guerrilla campaign, multi-party peace talks mired in divisive wrangling and fresh calls by the Irish government for Britain to listen to new evidence about the killings.

The Dublin government, Britain's partner in the search for a Northern Ireland settlement, is to collate evidence in a new book and academic study which are at variance with the 1972 findings of Lord Widgery, Britain's then Chief Justice.

A book by Don Mullan purports to prove that some of the dead were shot by a sniper or snipers on the walls of Northern Ireland's second city in direct contradiction of British assertions that only troops on the ground fired their guns.

Dermot Walsh, professor of Law at Limerick University, said last week that some of the evidence by soldiers given directly after the shootings was never presented to the official inquiry and suggested that it had been a whitewash.
The occasion is still a rallying call for Catholics who say they are treated as second class citizens by the British government and the Protestant majority which wants the province to remain British.

But it has underlined divisions between Sinn Fein, the militant voice of Irish nationalism, and the more moderate Catholic-backed Social Democratic and Labour Party of John Hume, a tireless peace-broker based in Londonderry.

Hume repeatedly called over the weekend for a new IRA ceasefire to win entry to the Belfast peace talks for Sinn Fein but the party's spokesmen say the London government has made impossible preconditions.

Adams wants an IRA truce to win automatic entry to the talks for Sinn Fein but Major says the ceasefire must be verifiably permanent and mark a complete end to the guerrilla campaign at the heart of a conflict which has killed 3,200 people.
